clue.text: * Flowery proliferation

parts.note: the only words printed: a botanical term for a flower spike that sprouts buds and grows on beyond itself
the star marks the competition word, which Azed gives with a bare definition for solvers to write their own clue

explanation.walkthrough: This is the Azed competition puzzle: the starred entry gets only a definition, and entrants send in their own clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The botanical term names abnormal growth in which a flower axis keeps sprouting fresh buds, a proliferation of the flower.

clue.text: Ticked off youngster giving up Latin

indicators.note: to give something up is to let it go, so that letter drops out of the word

parts.note: a child is a youngster
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A child gets a telling-off for abandoning Latin lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: CHID is an old past tense of chide, as Chambers allows.
explanation.definitionFit: To chide is to scold, so the old past tense means scolded, a telling-off already delivered.

clue.text: Swell without a blemish

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside, without means the following word wraps around the letter

parts.note: a blot is a stain or blemish
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hopes to swell up without a spot on their skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as 'lacking', but here it carries its older sense of 'outside'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bloat is to swell up or puff out, so the verbs are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Boggy tract, bit of land to eat away

indicators.note: only a small bit of the next word is wanted, namely its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of land
acid etches metal by eating it away

explanation.surface: Marshland slowly eats away at a patch of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Letch is a dialect word for a wet, boggy stretch of ground or a muddy ditch.

clue.text: Exchanging money, being absorbed by the Mona Lisa?

indicators.note: what is absorbed sits deep inside its host, so only a run from within the title survives and its outer letters fall away

parts.note: the painting's Italian title is La Gioconda

explanation.surface: Money changing hands is somehow swallowed up by Leonardo's famous portrait.
explanation.walkthrough: The host is not printed: the question mark asks you to swap the Mona Lisa for its Italian name, La Gioconda, then find the word inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Agio is the premium or charge paid when changing one currency for another, the business of exchanging money.

clue.text: Using pedals, long involved in awkward gradient

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within the other
an awkward arrangement is a clumsy one, so the letters are put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for long

explanation.surface: A cyclist toils at the pedals for a long time on a tough slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadle is a foot pedal driving a machine, so treadling is working it with the feet.

clue.text: Forced out, extra was member of cast

parts.note: ex. is a dictionary abbreviation for extra
a cast member is someone who acted in the play

explanation.surface: A film extra who had a part in the cast was pushed out of the job.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact is to extort or demand by force, so exacted means forced out of someone.

clue.text: Leg trapped in twisted tin case

indicators.note: something trapped in a container is held inside it, so one piece is enclosed by the other
a twisted word is bent out of its usual shape, so its letters change order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
crus is the anatomical Latin term for the leg between knee and ankle

explanation.surface: A leg gets stuck inside a bent tin can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a noun for the tin, but it is a verb: to encase.
explanation.definitionFit: To incrust is to cover with a hard coating, which is to encase something in a shell.

clue.text: Scratch regional runner such as S.Ovett, black

parts.note: Steve Cram, S. Cram, was a British middle-distance runner of the same era and the same first name as Steve Ovett
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A northern runner like Steve Ovett is described as dark-haired and scratching at the track.
explanation.walkthrough: Ovett and Cram were rival British milers of the 1980s, both called Steve, so 'such as S.Ovett' points to S. Cram.
explanation.definitionFit: Scramb is a dialect verb meaning to scratch or scrape with the nails, hence the regional label.

clue.text: Group of cooperative communities designed from earthy plans

indicators.note: something designed from materials is built anew out of them, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A set of communes is laid out according to down-to-earth blueprints.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourier's utopian scheme organised people into phalanxes, and a phalanstery is such a cooperative community or group of them.

clue.text: Husband on stage in afternoon, displaying calmness

indicators.note: in places the first group inside the abbreviation for the time of day

parts.note: p.m. marks the afternoon
H is the abbreviation for husband
a stage of a journey or race is a leg

explanation.surface: A husband appearing in an afternoon show keeps his composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places H before the stage word.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlegm in its old sense of the cool humour means imperturbable composure, a synonym for calmness.

clue.text: Forced to fit vineyards in assuming various shapes

indicators.note: in tells us the first item sits inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: Proteus the sea god could change his form at will
crus are French vineyards or their wines, as in grand cru

explanation.surface: Vineyards are made to adapt to all sorts of shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Procrustes stretched or lopped his guests to fit his bed, so the adjective describes enforcing conformity ruthlessly.

clue.text: Nip power off edge

indicators.note: off means removed, so that letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: to nip is to pinch
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut the electricity from a border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edge' is a verb here: to move little by little.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch forward is to move slowly and carefully, just as one edges along a ledge.

clue.text: Former extravagance — or is it misplaced energy?

indicators.note: misplaced things are put in the wrong spots, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether past excess was really just wasted energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' marks a word now obsolete; Spenser used it.
explanation.definitionFit: Riotise is an old word for riotous living, wild unrestrained excess and extravagant indulgence.

clue.text: Accountants as a group gathering SA currency as capital

indicators.note: to gather something is to take it in, so the first group holds the next piece

parts.note: ACCA is the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants
R stands for the rand, South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: A firm of accountants raises South African money to use as capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' is read as money, but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the capital city of Ghana, on the West African coast.

clue.text: Oriole of a kind from a Southeast Asian island in a package of goods

indicators.note: in places the island inside the bundle that follows

parts.note: a bale is a bundle of goods
Timor is an island in the Malay Archipelago

explanation.surface: An exotic bird arrives from a far island in a shipping crate.
explanation.definitionFit: The orange and black North American songbird is named after Lord Baltimore, whose heraldic colours it shares.

clue.text: Teething toy, see, to do with the mouth

parts.note: the letter C is pronounced the same as see
oral means relating to the mouth

explanation.surface: A baby's teething ring is all about the mouth, you see.
explanation.definitionFit: A stick of polished coral was once given to babies to chew while cutting their teeth.

clue.text: Errand boy once pocketing two articles in lathe accessory

indicators.note: to pocket something is to put it away inside, so the old word holds the others

parts.note: cad once meant an errand boy or odd-job helper
the and a are the definite and indefinite articles

explanation.surface: A former messenger slips a couple of items into a workshop machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathead is a sleeve or collar fitted on a lathe to steady work, so it is a lathe accessory.

clue.text: Fabulous bird, tailless kind

indicators.note: a creature with no tail has lost its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: kind as in humane, showing human kindness

explanation.surface: A legendary bird of a gentle kind that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from fable, not marvellous.
explanation.definitionFit: The huma is a mythical Persian bird said to never land and to bring good fortune.

clue.text: Deter wandering round island for fish to eat (9, two words)

indicators.note: round says the rearranged letters surround the island
a wandering path strays from its course, so the letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Mull is an island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides

explanation.surface: Someone tries to discourage roaming around an island in search of food fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The red mullet is a prized Mediterranean food fish, hence one to eat.

clue.text: Feature of culottes that often accompanies hose

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pair of identical letters, as the double letter in the middle of that word
second meaning: the close-fitting jacket worn with hose by Elizabethan men

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about clothes, so one looks for a garment in culottes; the feature is the pair of Ts in the spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a pair of matching letters and the jacket in the phrase 'doublet and hose'.

clue.text: Unruly sultan, eastern, once free of bounds

indicators.note: an unruly crowd will not keep order, so these letters break ranks

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
E is the abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: A disorderly eastern ruler used to roam without limits.
explanation.walkthrough: UNLASTE is Spenser's spelling of unlaced; 'once' marks it as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlaced means with the laces or ties undone, loosened and so freed of whatever bound it.

clue.text: Is shed what may start a blaze?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, as liquid flows over and is lost
second meaning: thin strips of wood or twisted paper used to light a fire

explanation.walkthrough: 'Is shed' suggests a garden building; it is the verb for being spilt.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for overflowing and a plural noun for the paper tapers used as fire-lighters.

clue.text: Remedies one restricts swallowing very small amount

parts.note: an, like a, means one

indicators.note: whatever swallows something takes it inside, so the verb's letters enclose the tiny amount

parts.note: to tie is to restrict
a dot is a tiny quantity

explanation.surface: A patient is limited to a tiny dose of medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Antidotes are substances that counteract poisons, so they are remedies or cures.

clue.text: S-sweet local chat?

parts.note: the stammered opening letter of the next word
pud is short for pudding, a sweet course

explanation.surface: Someone stammers over a sweet piece of local gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chat' looks like gossip, but in dialect a chat is a small potato. The question mark flags the twist.
explanation.definitionFit: In regional English a chat is a small potato, and a spud is the everyday word for any potato.

clue.text: This month is soaking up sun in a flash

indicators.note: something that soaks up another takes it in, so the date abbreviation encloses the next piece

parts.note: inst. is the old business-letter abbreviation for dates in the current month
a tan is what the sun gives the skin, and to sun is to tan

explanation.surface: This month someone is lying out, quickly catching the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant is a moment of time so short it passes like a flash.

clue.text: Creed forming closure of discourse in temporary pulpit

indicators.note: in places that single letter inside the shelter that follows

parts.note: a tent is a portable pulpit used for outdoor preaching, especially in Scotland

indicators.note: the closure of something is its very end, so only its final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of discourse

explanation.surface: A doctrine is set out at the end of a sermon in a field pulpit.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland a tent was a temporary wooden pulpit for open-air services.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief held as true, one article of a creed.

clue.text: Source of middle eastern verse, say, to continue once the sun goes in

definitions.text: Source of middle eastern verse, say

indicators.note: something that goes in enters another word, as the sun goes behind a cloud

parts.note: aby is an archaic form of abide, to continue or endure
Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: Eastern poetry is said to continue at dusk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes in' sounds like the sun clouding over, but it puts the sun inside the old word.
explanation.definitionFit: Araby is a poetic name for Arabia, the homeland of much middle eastern poetry, given as an example.

clue.text: Pipe I'll fill a little? Reverse of that

indicators.note: the answer is the result read backwards, the reverse of what was just built
to fill something is to sit inside it, so the single letter goes into the little amount

parts.note: a bit means a little
read as I will: the letter I, with will as the auxiliary for the verb that follows

explanation.surface: A musician says they will top up a pipe a bit, or do the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll fill a little' builds a word; the final instruction turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia was a Roman flute or reed pipe, and the shinbone took its name from it.

clue.text: Sediment that's formed in double espresso

indicators.note: the answer is formed inside the following words, using their letters as they stand

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Grounds collect at the bottom of a strong double coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Lees are the dregs that settle at the bottom of wine or other liquid, a kind of sediment.

clue.text: Scots ale making one sick, finishing off yard

indicators.note: finishing off another piece means coming after it, so this part is placed second

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for yard
one who is sick is ill

explanation.surface: Scottish beer that makes a drinker poorly, ending a night in the yard.
explanation.definitionFit: Yill is the Scots form of the word for ale, the brewed malt drink.

clue.text: Measure island denied land for island

parts.note: an ell is an old measure of cloth length

indicators.note: a word denied part of itself has that part refused it, so those letters go

parts.note: taken as written, before trimming
taken as written, the part removed

explanation.surface: Someone measures an island that has been refused territory in exchange for another island.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellis Island in New York harbour was the immigration station for the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellis is an island in New York harbour, famed as the entry point for immigrants.

clue.text: Playing in opera alfresco

indicators.note: playing around with something means fiddling with its arrangement, so the letters move

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer performs in an opera staged outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfresco is Italian for in the fresh air, so it means outdoors.

clue.text: Guinness? One served by clubs

parts.note: an ale is a drink served in a pub
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: A pint of Guinness is a drink handed out at clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Guinness looks like the stout, but it is the actor Sir Alec Guinness; the question mark warns of the switch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Alec Guinness was the British actor, so his first name is defined by his surname.

clue.text: One insect devouring another from behind in ineffective style

indicators.note: a creature devouring another takes it inside, so the first piece holds the second

parts.note: a fly is an insect

indicators.note: approaching from behind means reading the second insect from its back end

parts.note: another insect, a bee

explanation.surface: A predatory insect attacks another from the rear, rather half-heartedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Feebly is the adverb meaning weakly, without force, done in an ineffective manner.

clue.text: Shifting settlers yet influenced by urban culture (11, two words)

indicators.note: shifting things move about, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Migrating settlers still pick up the city's ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Street style describes fashion drawn from what young city dwellers wear rather than from designer houses.
